projects.title: Foundations of Computational Neuroscience
projects.summary: This repository demonstrates implementation of core computational neuroscience methods spanning biophysical neuron modeling, neural encoding and decoding theory, sensory transduction circuits, and spike-train–based system identification. Projects include simulations of Hodgkin–Huxley–type neurons, phase response curve analysis, integrate-and-fire encoding frameworks, divisive normalization models, olfactory and photoreceptor cascades, and direction-selective visual motion detection networks.
projects.description:
This repository contains coursework and projects from two graduate-level computational neuroscience courses at Columbia focused on building mechanistic neural circuit models and recovering system structure from spike timing data.

The modeling work includes conductance-based neuron simulations such as Hodgkin–Huxley, Connor–Stevens, Morris–Lecar, and Rinzel reductions. Analyses include F–I characterization, limit-cycle behavior, bifurcation across input currents, and numerical phase-response curve estimation using Winfree’s method and iPRC-based reductions.

Several projects implement time-encoding machine frameworks using integrate-and-fire neurons and asynchronous sigma–delta modulators. Signals are reconstructed from spike timing using Gram-matrix decoding methods, pseudoinverse solutions, and compensation-principle formulations, with reconstruction quality evaluated using SNR across stimulus classes.

The repository also explores sensory transduction pathways including Drosophila photoreceptor models, olfactory receptor cascades, and divisive normalization circuits, along with full OTP-to-biophysical spike-generator cascades comparing Connor–Stevens and Hodgkin–Huxley responses.

A larger visual-system project implements a directionally selective small-target motion detector inspired by insect vision, including retina preprocessing, lamina temporal filtering, ON/OFF channel separation, medulla delay circuits, and lobula correlation-based motion detection.

Across projects, spike-train data are used to reconstruct unknown dendritic filters using trig-polynomial stimulus spaces, Φ-matrix formulations, and regularized least-squares solutions, demonstrating practical experience with neural system identification from event-based observations.
